solution:
Rainfall.
The air carrying water vapour cools as it rises, the vapour condenses into droplets, and when the droplets become too heavy to float in the air they come down as rainfall. We generally get our water in this form, and agriculture in India depends to a large extent on the Monsoon rainfall.

Fog.
When the temperature of the air near the earth's surface falls, the vapour condenses into microscopic water particles that float in the air. When the density of these droplets increases, fog occurs and visibility is greatly reduced. In London there is such fog till the afternoons in the winters.

Hail (hailstones).
Hail does not occur in equatorial areas because of the heat in the atmosphere. These big, heavy hailstones fall rapidly to the ground and may destroy the standing crops.

Snowfall.
When the temperature in the atmosphere falls below the freezing point, water vapour turns directly into snowflakes, and this precipitation in the form of solid particles of snow settles in layers on the ground. It occurs in high latitudinal and temperate regions and at high altitudes, so it is not experienced in Maharashtra.

| Figure | Rainfall type |
|---|---|
| A | Convectional rainfall |
| B | Orographic rainfall |
| C | Cyclonic rainfall |

In figure A the arrows show the heated air rising straight upwards while heavy rain falls from thick dark clouds, which is what happens in convectional rainfall. In figure B moisture-laden winds coming from the water body are obstructed by a mountain and are forced to rise along its slope, so heavy rain falls on that slope and only a little beyond the peak; this is orographic rainfall. In figure C the air moves in horizontally towards the centre of a low pressure area and then rises in a spiral, giving rain over the area the cyclone passes; this is cyclonic rainfall.

It is raining more on the windward side of the mountain, that is the left-hand slope in fig B, the side facing the water body from which the moist winds are blowing. Thick clouds and heavy rain are shown over this slope. The moisture-laden winds are obstructed by the mountain and start going upwards along its slope, their temperature drops, condensation takes place and rainfall occurs. That is why the windward side of the mountains gets more rain.

The rain shadow region lies on the leeward side of the mountain in fig B, that is the whole right-hand part of the figure beyond the summit: the long right slope and the low ground stretching away from it, where only a small cloud with a few light rain streaks is drawn. Shade that entire area to the right of the peak. It is called the rain-shadow area. The winds lose most of their moisture while rising along the windward slope, so after crossing the mountain the amount of vapour in the air reduces and the moisture holding capacity of the air increases; hence this side gets much less rainfall.

Figure A shows convectional rainfall and figure C shows cyclonic rainfall. In A the surface is heated by the sun's heat, so the air near it also gets heated, spreads, becomes lighter and moves straight upwards; it cools as it rises, the vapour condenses and rain falls, almost daily in the afternoons and accompanied by lightning and thunder. In C there is an area where the air pressure is less than in the surrounding regions, which is called a cyclone; air from the surrounding region comes towards the centre of the cyclone and then starts moving upwards, cools, and rainfall takes place. So in A it is the heating of the surface that makes the air rise, while in C it is the low pressure at the centre that draws the air in and lifts it. Convectional rainfall occurs in a very limited area of the world, whereas it rains over all the areas the cyclone passes over and a cyclone's area is quite extensive.

Stormy winds and floods are associated with cyclonic rainfall, shown in figure C. The cyclonic rainfall occurring in the tropical regions is limited in extent and is stormy in nature. Cyclonic rainfall is also less certain than convectional rainfall, and therefore such areas are frequently prone to very heavy rainfall and floods.

Convectional rainfall, the type shown in figure A. Singapore lies in the equatorial belt, and in equatorial areas the surface and the air above it get strongly heated, so the light air rises, cools and gives rainfall almost daily in the afternoons, accompanied by lightning and thunder.
[Note: the chapter does not mention Singapore anywhere. It only states that convectional rainfall occurs in equatorial areas, and names the Congo basin of Africa and the Amazon basin of South America as examples.]

Acid rain is the odd man out.
Orographic rainfall, cyclonic rainfall and convectional rainfall are the three types of rainfall described in the chapter, and each of them is named after the way in which the moist air is made to rise. Acid rain is not a type of this kind. It is rainfall whose water carries dissolved acids such as nitric acid and sulphuric acid, formed when the water vapour in the air reacts chemically with the gases released by air pollution in industrial areas, and it is harmful to living organisms as well as to non-living objects.

Dew is the odd man out.
Snowfall, rainfall and hailstones are the major forms of precipitation, in which water falls from the clouds to the ground in the solid or the liquid state. Dew does not fall from the clouds at all. It forms right at the earth's surface, when moisture-laden air near the surface comes into contact with very cold objects, the vapour condenses, and the very small water droplets stick to the surface of those cold objects.

The anemometer is the odd man out.
The other three are connected with rainfall and the factors that decide it. The rain gauge is the instrument used to measure rainfall, the measuring jar is used to measure the rainwater collected in the gauge, and the thermometer measures temperature, which the chapter names as one of the factors affecting the amount of rainfall in a region. An anemometer measures the speed of the wind, and wind speed has no part in the measurement of rainfall.
[Note: the chapter does not mention the anemometer or the thermometer at all; only the rain gauge and the measuring jar are described in it.]

Precipitation means water falling from the clouds to the ground in the solid or the liquid state. It occurs on the earth in three major forms: snow, hail and rainfall. Snowfall occurs when the temperature in the atmosphere falls below the freezing point and the water vapour turns directly into snowflakes, a change called sublimation. Hail occurs when a fast upward flow of air carries the condensed water droplets to a higher altitude where they solidify, gather layer upon layer and fall as big heavy hailstones. Rainfall occurs when the rising air cools, the vapour condenses, the droplets and dust particles gather into clouds, and the droplets grow so heavy that they can no longer float in the air. When condensation takes place near the earth's surface itself, we see fog, dew and frost instead.

The rain shadow area is the region on the leeward side of a mountain, that is the side away from the moisture-laden winds. Very little rainfall occurs here. The winds give up most of their moisture as rain while they are rising along the windward slope, so the amount of vapour in the air reduces after crossing the mountain. Beyond the mountain the moisture holding capacity of this air increases, so condensation hardly takes place and hardly any rain falls. That is why this comparatively dry region is identified as the rain-shadow area.

Orographic rainfall occurs in most of the parts of the world. Winds coming from the seas and the lakes are moisture-laden, and high mountain ranges lie in the path of such winds in most parts of the world. Wherever the winds are obstructed in this way they start going upwards along the slope of the mountains, their temperature drops, condensation occurs and rainfall takes place. The other two types are far more restricted: convectional rainfall is regional in nature and occurs in a very limited area, mainly the equatorial belt, while cyclonic rainfall occurs more in the temperate zones and is limited in extent in the tropical regions. The rainfall that India receives from the Monsoon winds is also of the orographic type.

When the condensation or solidification of the water vapour in the atmosphere occurs near the earth's surface, fog, dew and frost become visible. Fog is seen when the temperature of the air near the surface reduces, the vapour condenses into microscopic water particles that float in the air, and the density of these droplets increases. Dew is seen when moisture-laden air near the earth's surface comes into contact with very cold objects, the vapour condenses, and the very small water droplets stick to the surface of those objects. Frost is seen when the temperature of the air is less than 0°C, so that these water droplets sticking to the cold objects freeze. Dew and frost occur on a large scale in the winters.

The rain gauge should be kept in open ground, so that the rainwater is collected without any obstruction. It should be placed on a flat mound about 30 cm high. The funnel fitted to the gauge must be of the specific diameter fixed for it, so that the rain falling into it is properly collected in the bottle below. The water collected in the bottle should then be measured with the help of the measuring jar, which reads in millimetres. In areas of heavy rainfall the reading of the rain should be taken every three hours.

| Dew | Frost |
|---|---|
| It forms when moisture-laden air near the earth's surface comes into contact with very cold objects and the vapour condenses. | It forms when the temperature of the air is less than 0°C, so that the water droplets stuck to the surface of cold objects freeze. |
| It is in the liquid state — very small water droplets sticking to the surface of the cold objects. | It is in the solid state — the frozen water droplets. |
| Dew damages some crops by spreading diseases, though it may be beneficial to some crops. | Frost is harmful to crops and causes accidents if it is spread on the road. |

Both dew and frost occur on a large scale in the winters.

| Snow | Hail |
|---|---|
| It forms when the temperature in the atmosphere falls below the freezing point and the water vapour turns directly into snowflakes. This change of gas into solid is called sublimation. | It forms when strong heating of the earth's surface makes the air flow upwards at great speed, the vapour condenses, dark clouds form, and the droplets carried to a higher altitude solidify into hailstones. |
| The snow settles quietly in layers on the ground, and as it is in the solid form it does not flow like water. | The hailstones are taken upwards again and again by the upward flow of air, a new layer of snow encapsulates the hail each time, so concentric layers are formed and the hail grows in size before falling rapidly to the ground because of gravity. |
| Snowfall occurs at the mean sea level in high latitudinal and temperate regions, and in tropical areas only at places higher than the snowline. | Hail occurs in the summers in India, Africa and some parts of South East Asia. It does not occur in equatorial areas because of the heat in the atmosphere, nor in the cold zones because of the lack of upward flow. |
| When snow accumulates on a large scale the transport and communication system of that area collapses and people have to protect themselves from frostbite; when the snow melts, the region gets water. | Because of hail, crops may get destroyed and loss of life and property may also occur. |
